# 12-Week Prenatal Strength Programme

**Client Profile:** 30 y/o, advanced lifter, starting at 20 weeks gestation, finishing at 32 weeks. Full gym access. OB-cleared for moderate strength training.

## Guiding Principles

- **No supine work** (no flat bench, no flat-back floor pressing/crunching). Use incline benches set to 15–30° minimum throughout.
- **No 1RM testing or max singles.** Cap loads at RPE 7 (3+ reps in reserve). No grinders, no failure.
- **Talk test as the cardio governor.** She should be able to hold a conversation through working sets.
- **Avoid Valsalva.** Exhale through the sticking point, no breath holding beyond 1–2 seconds.
- **Wide stance, neutral spine** on all hinges and squats as the bump grows. Expect to swap barbell hinges for trap bar / DB by week 28+ as the belly interferes.
- **Daily pelvic floor + diaphragmatic breathing** (5 min). Coordinate inhale on eccentric, exhale on concentric.
- **Watch for:** SI pain, pubic symphysis pain (avoid single-leg/staggered if it flares), diastasis coning, dizziness when changing positions, leaking, Braxton-Hicks during sets. Stop and reassess if any appear.
- **Session frequency:** 4 strength days/week, 2–3 easy aerobic days (incline walk, bike, swim). Aim for ~150 min moderate cardio/week per ACOG.
- **Warm-up template (10 min):** cat-cow, 90/90 breathing, hip CARs, band pull-aparts, glute bridges (off floor early, regress to standing hip thrusts later), bodyweight squats.

---

## PHASE 1 — Strength Maintenance (Weeks 1–4 / Gestation 20–23)

Goal: Establish the new template, dial in RPE, keep her feeling strong. She still has good mechanics in most lifts.

**4-day split: Upper / Lower / Upper / Lower**

### Day A — Upper (Push Bias)
- Incline DB press (30°): 4×6–8 @ RPE 6–7
- Chest-supported row: 4×8–10
- Seated DB overhead press: 3×8
- Half-kneeling cable row: 3×10/side
- Incline DB fly: 2×12
- Pallof press: 3×10/side

### Day B — Lower (Squat Bias)
- Goblet squat or SSB squat: 4×6–8 @ RPE 6–7
- Hip thrust (back on bench, not floor): 4×8
- Walking lunge (DB): 3×8/leg
- Seated leg curl: 3×10
- Standing calf raise: 3×12
- Suitcase carry: 3×30 sec/side

### Day C — Upper (Pull Bias)
- Lat pulldown (neutral grip): 4×8
- Landmine press (standing): 4×6/side
- Single-arm DB row: 3×10/side
- Incline DB curl: 3×10
- Cable triceps pushdown: 3×12
- Side plank (modified, knee down): 3×20–30 sec/side

### Day D — Lower (Hinge Bias)
- Trap bar deadlift: 4×5 @ RPE 7
- Bulgarian split squat: 3×8/leg
- 45° back extension: 3×10
- Step-up (knee-height): 3×8/leg
- Cable pull-through: 3×12
- Bird dog: 3×8/side

**Weekly progression:** Week 1 baseline → add 2.5–5 lb to main lifts each week if RPE stays ≤7 and movement quality holds.

---

## PHASE 2 — Adaptation & Substitution (Weeks 5–8 / Gestation 24–27)

Goal: Begin swapping movements that the bump interferes with. Reduce volume slightly, hold intensity at RPE 6–7. This is when many clients start losing range on conventional barbell lifts.

**Key swaps:**
- Trap bar replaces all conventional barbell deadlifts
- All squats from front rack or goblet (bar in back can become uncomfortable; let her choose)
- DB/landmine replaces any barbell pressing she finds awkward
- Lunges → reverse lunges (better balance, less SI shear)

### Day A — Upper Push
- Incline barbell press (45°): 4×6 @ RPE 7
- Half-kneeling landmine press: 3×8/side
- Chest-supported T-bar row: 4×8
- Seated cable row: 3×10
- Face pull: 3×15
- Dead bug with band: 3×8/side

### Day B — Lower Squat
- Front-rack goblet or front squat: 4×5 @ RPE 7
- B-stance hip thrust: 3×8/side
- Reverse lunge (DB): 3×8/leg
- Leg extension: 3×12
- Standing calf raise: 3×12
- Farmer's carry: 3×40 sec

### Day C — Upper Pull
- Neutral-grip pull-down or assisted pull-up: 4×6–8
- Incline DB press (light, 2nd press day): 3×10
- Meadows row or single-arm cable row: 3×10/side
- Hammer curl: 3×10
- Overhead triceps extension: 3×12
- Copenhagen plank (short lever): 3×15 sec/side

### Day D — Lower Hinge
- Trap bar deadlift: 4×5 @ RPE 7
- Single-leg RDL (light DB, supported): 3×8/leg
- 45° back extension: 3×12
- Goblet box squat: 3×8
- Cable pull-through: 3×12
- Side plank (full or modified): 3×20–30 sec/side

**Volume:** ~10% less total reps than Phase 1. Add load only if RPE allows and bump isn't impeding bar path.

---

## PHASE 3 — Deload & Reposition (Weeks 9–12 / Gestation 28–31)

Goal: Shift to a "stay strong, stay mobile, prep for labour" model. By week 30+ many lifts need machine or DB versions. Drop to 3 strength days + more walking. Intensity caps at RPE 6. Focus on posterior chain, upper back, hip mobility, and breath mechanics — all directly useful for birth and postpartum recovery.

**3-day full-body split: Mon / Wed / Fri**

### Day 1 — Full Body Strength
- Goblet box squat: 3×6 @ RPE 6
- Incline DB press (45°+): 3×8
- Chest-supported row: 3×10
- 45° back extension: 3×10
- Standing Pallof press: 3×10/side
- Suitcase carry: 3×30 sec/side

### Day 2 — Full Body (Hinge Focus)
- Trap bar deadlift (or KB deadlift if trap bar awkward): 3×5 @ RPE 6
- B-stance hip thrust: 3×8/side
- Half-kneeling landmine press: 3×8/side
- Seated cable row: 3×10
- Cable pull-through: 3×12
- Side-lying clamshells with band: 2×15/side

### Day 3 — Full Body (Accessory & Mobility)
- Heels-elevated goblet squat: 3×8
- Single-arm DB bench (incline 45°): 3×8/side
- Lat pulldown: 3×10
- Step-up (mid-shin box): 3×8/leg
- Cable wood-chop (horizontal, not rotational under load): 3×10/side
- Deep squat hold with breathing: 3×30–45 sec

**Cardio:** Replace one strength session with a longer easy walk if she's fatigued. Prenatal yoga or swimming 1–2x/week is ideal here.

**Week 12 wind-down:** If she's still feeling great, hold the template. If fatigue/pelvic pressure ramps up, drop loads another 10–20% and shift more time to mobility, breath work, and walking. She'll thank you postpartum.

---

## Recovery & Adjuncts

- **Sleep:** Side-lying (left preferred), pillow between knees. Aim 8+ hours.
- **Hydration:** ~3L/day, more if training in heat.
- **Protein:** Roughly 1.6–1.8 g/kg bodyweight (using pre-pregnancy weight as the baseline). Spread across 4 meals.
- **Iron, calcium, omega-3, prenatal vitamin** — defer specifics to her OB/dietitian.
- **Mobility (daily 10 min):** 90/90 hip switches, deep squat breathing, thoracic openers, cat-cow.
- **Pelvic floor work:** Daily diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor relaxation on inhale, gentle lift on exhale. Coordinate with lifts. Consider a referral to a pelvic floor PT now — invaluable for the postpartum return.

---

## Red Flags — Stop Training & Call OB

Vaginal bleeding, regular painful contractions, amniotic fluid leakage, dyspnoea before exertion, dizziness, headache, chest pain, calf pain/swelling, or decreased fetal movement. Print the ACOG list and post it in her training file.

Let me know her starting numbers on the main lifts and I'll plug in specific loads for Week 1.

# Prenatal Nutrition Plan — Lean Mass Maintenance

Designed to pair with the 12-week programme. Goals: support fetal growth, maintain maternal lean mass through a period where training volume drops, manage energy without excessive fat gain, and set her up for postpartum recovery and (if she chooses) lactation.

**Important caveat:** Any specific supplementation, caloric targets, or restrictions should be cleared with her OB and ideally a prenatal RD. This is a training-side framework, not medical advice.

---

## Caloric Framework

Pregnancy energy needs rise modestly. ACOG / IOM guidance for a normal-BMI client:

- **Trimester 1 (already past):** +0 kcal/day
- **Trimester 2 (weeks 13–27):** +340 kcal/day above maintenance
- **Trimester 3 (weeks 28–40):** +450 kcal/day above maintenance

She's training hard, so she sits at the top of these ranges. **Practical starting point:**

- **Weeks 1–4 of programme (gestation 20–23):** maintenance + 350 kcal
- **Weeks 5–8 (gestation 24–27):** maintenance + 400 kcal
- **Weeks 9–12 (gestation 28–31):** maintenance + 450 kcal

If she was eating ~2,200 kcal pre-pregnancy at maintenance, she's now in the **2,550–2,650 kcal/day** range. Adjust by weight gain trajectory (see below), not by the scale daily.

### Weight Gain Target (IOM)
For a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5–24.9): **25–35 lb total** across pregnancy, roughly **0.75–1 lb/week in T2 and T3**. If she's gaining faster than ~1.25 lb/week sustained, trim 150–200 kcal. If gaining under 0.5 lb/week, add 200 kcal. Don't react to single weigh-ins — use 2-week trends.

---

## Macronutrient Targets

### Protein — the lean mass lever
- **Target: 1.6–1.8 g/kg of pre-pregnancy bodyweight**, plus ~25 g/day for fetal/placental demand in T2–T3.
- For a 65 kg client that's roughly **125–140 g/day**.
- **Distribution: 30–40 g per meal across 4 meals.** Leucine threshold matters more when training volume is lower — even doses drive MPS better than skewed ones.
- Prioritise complete sources: eggs, dairy (Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, milk), poultry, fish (see mercury notes), lean beef, tofu/tempeh, whey isolate.

### Carbohydrates — fuel training and the fetus
- **Target: 4–5 g/kg/day** (~260–325 g for a 65 kg client).
- Brain glucose demand rises in T3; under-eating carbs causes early ketosis which isn't ideal during pregnancy.
- **Timing:** load the larger portion around training (pre + post). Slower-digesting sources at other meals to stabilise blood sugar — relevant for gestational diabetes risk.
- Sources: oats, rice, potatoes, sweet potato, fruit, whole grain bread/pasta, legumes.

### Fats — hormone and fetal brain development
- **Target: 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day** (~55–65 g), filling the remainder of calories.
- Emphasise **omega-3 (DHA specifically):** 200–300 mg DHA/day minimum. Two servings/week of low-mercury fatty fish (salmon, sardines, trout) or an algae-based DHA supplement.
- Olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, full-fat dairy.

### Fibre
- **28–30 g/day.** Constipation is a major T3 complaint and progesterone slows GI motility. Build through veg, fruit (berries, pears), oats, chia, legumes.

### Fluids
- **3–3.5 L/day**, more on training days or in heat. Add electrolytes (sodium especially) around sessions — blood volume is up ~45% and she'll feel it.

---

## Sample Day (~2,600 kcal, ~135 g protein, ~290 g carbs, ~70 g fat)

**Breakfast (on waking, ~600 kcal)**
- 3 whole eggs + 2 whites scrambled
- 1 cup oats cooked in milk, topped with berries and 1 tbsp chia
- Coffee (cap caffeine at 200 mg/day total)

**Pre-training snack (~300 kcal)**
- Greek yogurt (200 g) with honey and a banana

**Training session**
- Sip electrolyte drink through workout (sodium ~500 mg, optional 20–30 g carbs if session runs long)

**Post-training lunch (~700 kcal)**
- 150 g grilled chicken or salmon
- 1.5 cups rice or potato
- Large mixed salad with olive oil
- Fruit on the side

**Afternoon snack (~350 kcal)**
- Cottage cheese (200 g) with pineapple, handful of walnuts
- Or: whey isolate shake + apple + almond butter

**Dinner (~650 kcal)**
- 150 g lean beef, tofu, or fish
- Roasted sweet potato + 2 cups roasted veg
- Avocado, olive oil

**Evening (optional, especially T3)**
- Warm milk or Greek yogurt with a sprinkle of granola — slow protein before sleep supports overnight MPS and can ease early-morning nausea/heartburn.

---

## Training-Day vs Rest-Day Adjustments

- **Training days:** keep the higher carb total (~300 g), pre + post emphasis.
- **Rest days:** drop carbs ~50 g, raise fat ~15 g to hold calories. Keep protein identical.

---

## Foods to Limit or Avoid

**Avoid entirely:**
- Alcohol
- Raw/undercooked meat, eggs, fish (no sushi with raw fish, no rare steak)
- Unpasteurised dairy and juices, soft unpasteurised cheeses (brie, feta unless labelled pasteurised)
- Deli meats unless heated (listeria risk)
- High-mercury fish: shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish, bigeye tuna
- Liver in large amounts (vitamin A toxicity risk)

**Limit:**
- Caffeine to **<200 mg/day** (~one 12 oz coffee)
- Albacore tuna to 6 oz/week
- Added sugars — relevant for GD prevention
- Highly processed foods crowding out nutrient density

---

## Key Micronutrients (mostly covered by prenatal vitamin, but worth knowing)

| Nutrient | Why | Food sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Folate** (600 mcg) | Neural tube, ongoing cell division | Leafy greens, legumes, fortified grains |
| **Iron** (27 mg) | Blood volume expansion, anaemia prevention | Red meat, lentils, spinach + vitamin C |
| **Calcium** (1,000 mg) | Fetal skeleton, maternal bone | Dairy, fortified plant milks, sardines |
| **Vitamin D** (600+ IU) | Calcium absorption, immune | Fatty fish, fortified dairy, sun, supplement |
| **Choline** (450 mg) | Fetal brain development — under-consumed | Eggs (2 yolks = ~250 mg), beef, salmon |
| **DHA** (200–300 mg) | Fetal brain, eyes | Fatty fish, algae oil |
| **Iodine** (220 mcg) | Fetal thyroid/neurodevelopment | Iodised salt, dairy, seafood |

Most prenatals miss choline and DHA — flag these to her OB/RD.

---

## Phase-Specific Nutrition Notes

### Weeks 1–4 (Gestation 20–23)
Energy is usually best here. Build the habits: hit protein at every meal, pre-/post-training carb structure, hydration. Establish a weekly weigh-in (same day, same conditions). Get bloodwork baseline through OB if not already done — ferritin especially.

### Weeks 5–8 (Gestation 24–27)
Glucose tolerance test typically happens around week 24–28. If GD is diagnosed, the macro split shifts (lower carb, more even distribution, no large carb boluses) — we'd revise. Heartburn often begins; shift to **5–6 smaller meals** instead of 4 larger ones if needed. Avoid eating within 2 hours of bed.

### Weeks 9–12 (Gestation 28–31)
Stomach capacity drops as the uterus crowds it. **Smaller, more frequent meals** become essential. Liquid calories (smoothies, milk, kefir) get useful here. Protein remains non-negotiable — even if appetite drops, hit the number with shakes if needed. Constipation and reflux peak; emphasise fibre, fluids, magnesium glycinate (with OB approval), and elevation when sleeping.

---

## Supplement Stack (pending OB approval)

1. **Prenatal multivitamin** — daily, with food
2. **Algae-based DHA** 300 mg/day if fish intake is low
3. **Vitamin D3** 1,000–2,000 IU/day if levels are low (test first)
4. **Magnesium glycinate** 200–300 mg evening — sleep, cramps, constipation
5. **Whey isolate or pea protein** — practical tool to hit protein targets when appetite drops
6. **Electrolytes** around training — sodium-forward, not sugar-forward

## Intensity Techniques Explained

These let her train *hard* without chasing 1RM expressions:

- **Eccentric tempo (3-sec lowering):** Triples time under tension per rep, makes a moderate load feel genuinely heavy. Safest way to add stimulus in pregnancy.
- **Cluster sets:** Short intra-set rests let her hit high-quality reps with a heavier-feeling load while keeping bar speed up and Valsalva off the table. Each mini-set ends with reps in reserve.
- **Mechanical drop sets:** Switch to an easier variation of the same movement once the harder version stalls. More total work, no load chasing.
- **1.5 reps and paused work:** Brutal at moderate loads, very controlled, no peak force spike.
- **Tight rest on accessories:** Cardiovascular challenge without true intervals. The *feeling* of being smoked is achieved through density.

**What we deliberately don't use:**
- AMRAP / training to failure
- Heavy singles or doubles
- Drop sets on barbell main lifts (control matters too much)
- Plyometrics or jump work

# Pressing Programme — Working Around the Supine Restriction

She loves bench. Good news: there's a lot we can do. The flat barbell bench is out from week 16 onward, but **pressing volume and the *feeling* of bench pressing can be largely preserved** through smart angle and implement selection. The goal here is to make pressing day feel like pressing day — heavy, satisfying, lots of work — without ever putting her flat on her back.

This integrates into the existing programme: it expands what's already on the Day A (Upper Push) sessions and adds a few options to swap in across phases.

---

## Why No Flat Bench After Week 16

Two reasons, both legitimate:

1. **Vena cava compression.** Lying flat compresses the inferior vena cava under the weight of the uterus, reducing venous return, dropping maternal blood pressure, and reducing placental perfusion. Symptoms (dizziness, nausea, breathlessness) often appear, but not always — and the absence of symptoms doesn't mean perfusion is fine.
2. **Mechanical interference.** The bar path on a flat bench gets compromised as the belly grows, forcing compensations.

**The fix isn't to stop pressing — it's to elevate the torso.** A 15° incline is generally considered the minimum acceptable angle. **I'd recommend defaulting to 30° as a comfortable safety margin** and going steeper as pregnancy progresses.

- **Bench angle:** 30° default; bump up to 45° if reflux flares or if breathing under load feels restricted

- **Foot position:** feet flat on floor, knees slightly wider than normal as belly grows — gives the ribcage room
- **Bar path:** to the upper chest / collarbone area, not lower chest, on incline work
- **Breathing:** inhale on descent, **exhale through the press** — no breath holding. This is the single most important cue. A pre-pregnancy bench press uses Valsalva by default; she has to actively rewire this.
- **Brace:** 360° low-pressure brace (think "expand your ribs") rather than a hard belt-style brace. We're not bracing against intra-abdominal pressure; we're creating stability without it.
- **Coning check:** have her or you watch the midline on the first set. If the linea alba domes upward during the press, reduce the load, increase the incline, or switch to DBs.
- **No arch.** A big powerlifting arch is out — it shortens the range to the chest but adds lumbar extension stress that's already increased in pregnancy.

- **3-second eccentric every rep** — triples time under tension, makes 60% feel like 75%
- **Paused bench (1–2 sec on chest)** — kills the stretch reflex, true concentric strength
- **1.5 rep press** — full rep + half rep from chest = 1 rep. Brutal at light loads.
- **Cluster sets** — 3 reps, 20 sec rest, 3 reps, 20 sec rest, 3 reps. Heavier-feeling load, no failure, no breath holding
- **Mechanical drop set** — barbell low-incline → switch to DB → switch to push-up. One continuous extended set.
- **DB pause press** — 1-sec pause at bottom of every rep
- **Constant-tension press** — never lock out, keep elbows slightly bent throughout. Burns at light loads.

# Prenatal Core Programme

Smart instinct. A strong, well-coordinated core is one of the highest-leverage things she can train right now — it supports the spine under increasing anterior load, helps manage diastasis recti (which happens to *every* pregnancy to some degree, the goal is managing the degree), preserves the breath-pressure-pelvic floor system that labour and postpartum recovery depend on, and dramatically shortens the postpartum return to lifting.

But prenatal core work is not "more crunches, harder planks." It's a different system — and an advanced lifter often has to *unlearn* some bracing habits that served her in powerlifting but actively work against her now.

---

## The Core Strategy in Pregnancy

Three principles drive everything below:

**1. Train the deep system, not the six-pack.**
The rectus abdominis is going to stretch and separate — that's normal and unavoidable. What we *can* train is the deep stabilising system: transverse abdominis, pelvic floor, multifidus, and diaphragm working as a coordinated unit. This is the system that holds the trunk together during pregnancy and rebuilds the midline after.

**2. Manage intra-abdominal pressure, don't maximise it.**
Pre-pregnancy bracing is largely about *creating* high intra-abdominal pressure to stabilise heavy loads. Prenatal bracing is about *managing* pressure — generating just enough to stabilise, never so much that it pushes the linea alba outward (coning) or down through the pelvic floor (leaking, heaviness, prolapse risk). This is the single biggest mindset shift.

**3. Avoid anything that loads the midline into flexion or causes coning.**
Out: crunches, sit-ups, V-ups, hanging leg raises, toes-to-bar, ab wheel rollouts, full planks once coning appears, any supine core work after week 16. In: anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral flexion, carries, breath work, and deep stabiliser training.

---

## What Coning Is and Why It Governs Everything

Coning (or "doming") is when the midline of the abdomen pushes outward in a ridge or tent shape during effort. It's a sign that intra-abdominal pressure is exceeding what the linea alba can contain, and **repeated coning under load worsens diastasis recti.**

**How to check:** Have her look down at her belly during the hardest part of any core exercise (and any lift). If she sees a vertical ridge pushing forward, that movement is currently too hard for her core system at that load. **Regress it — don't push through.**

This check needs to happen weekly throughout the programme, not just on core exercises. Coning during a deadlift means the deadlift needs to be regressed too.

## The Four Core Categories She'll Train

### 1. Breath & Pressure Management (Foundation — Daily)

This is the actual heavy lifting of prenatal core work, even though it looks like nothing.

- **360° diaphragmatic breathing:** seated or side-lying, hands on lower ribs, inhale into the ribs expanding in all directions (front, sides, back), exhale fully and feel the lower abdomen gently draw in. 5 min daily.
- **Connection breath:** inhale and relax the pelvic floor, exhale and gently lift the pelvic floor + draw in the lower abdomen ("zip up from pubic bone to ribs"). Pair this exhale-lift with the concentric phase of every lift in the programme.
- **Blowing-out-a-candle exhale:** on the hardest part of any lift, exhale as if blowing out a candle slowly. This prevents breath-holding and keeps pressure managed.

### 2. Anti-Extension (Resists the spine arching backward)

The pregnant lumbar spine is already pulled into extension by the anterior load of the bump. Anti-extension work is the antidote to back pain and the foundation of trunk stability.

- Dead bug variations
- Bird dog
- Pallof press
- Half-kneeling press / chops
- Standing band rollouts (instead of ab wheel)
- Stability ball stir-the-pot (hands on ball, knees down)

### 3. Anti-Rotation (Resists the trunk being twisted)

The single most useful core quality for daily life with a growing bump (and later, holding a baby on one hip).

- Pallof press (all variations — standing, half-kneeling, tall-kneeling)
- Half-kneeling cable chop and lift
- Bird dog with band
- Single-arm carries (suitcase, racked)
- Single-arm pressing and rowing (already in the programme — count these)

### 4. Anti-Lateral Flexion (Resists side-bending)

Critical for SI joint stability and pelvic girdle pain prevention.

- Suitcase carry
- Side plank variations (modified as needed)
- Copenhagen plank (short lever)
- Single-arm farmer's carry
- Standing band side holds

## Cues for Every Core Exercise

- **Exhale on effort** — always. Inhale to set up, exhale through the hardest part.
- **Ribs down, not flared** — the ribcage should stack over the pelvis, not flare up
- **Pelvic floor lift on exhale** — gentle, not maximal. Think 30% effort, not 100%.
- **Watch the midline** — if you see coning, the exercise is too hard right now
- **Slow tempo** — speed is not a goal in prenatal core work
- **Neutral spine** — no posterior pelvic tilt cranking, no excessive arch

## Diastasis Recti — What to Tell Her

Every pregnant person develops some degree of midline separation by the third trimester. **This is anatomy doing its job**, not a failure of her core. The goal isn't to prevent it (you can't) — it's to:

1. Avoid making it worse through coning movements and high IAP work
2. Maintain deep stabiliser function so the system rebuilds well postpartum
3. Train the pattern of pressure management she'll use in labour and recovery

**Self-check (monthly):** lying on side (not supine), fingers pressed gently into the midline above, at, and below the navel during a small head lift. She's looking for a sense of how wide the gap is and whether she can generate tension across it. **The depth and tension matter more than the width.** A 3-finger gap with good tension is better than a 1-finger gap with no tension.

If she develops significant coning at rest, persistent doming, or back pain that doesn't respond to position changes — refer to a pelvic floor PT now, not postpartum. The waitlists are long and the work is invaluable.

## Pelvic Floor — The Other Half of the Core

Cannot overstate this: **the pelvic floor is core musculature.** She's training it whether she addresses it directly or not — the question is whether she trains it well.

- **Pelvic floor relaxation is as important as pelvic floor contraction.** A chronically tight pelvic floor is *not* a strong one — it's a dysfunctional one. Many advanced lifters have over-gripped pelvic floors from years of Valsalva bracing. Pregnancy is the time to retrain this.
- **Connection breath (described above) trains both** — relaxation on inhale, gentle lift on exhale.
- **Deep squat holds** (Phase 3) lengthen the pelvic floor — directly relevant to labour.
- **Refer to a pelvic floor PT.** Even one session prenatally is enormously valuable. They can assess her specific function and give targeted homework.

# No. And Here's Why.

I want to give you a straight answer because this matters: **a 1RM attempt at week 32 of pregnancy is contraindicated, and it's outside what her OB cleared.** Her referral specifies "moderate strength" and explicitly excludes max attempts. Programming a 1RM test would be working against her medical clearance.

I know that's not what you were hoping to hear, so let me explain the reasoning, then give you what a meaningful "peak week" *can* look like — because there's a real and satisfying answer here.

---

## Why a 1RM Is Off the Table at Week 32

**1. Valsalva is unavoidable at a true 1RM.**
A genuine max attempt requires maximal intra-abdominal pressure. There is no version of a 1RM bench, squat, or deadlift that doesn't involve significant breath-holding and IAP spikes. By week 32, that pressure has three places to go: up against the diaphragm (already compressed), out against the linea alba (already stretched, risking worsening DR), and down against the pelvic floor (already loaded by the weight of the uterus). All three are bad outcomes.

**2. Blood pressure spikes are dangerous in late pregnancy.**
1RM attempts produce transient BP spikes of 50+ mmHg systolic. At week 32, she's also at peak risk window for pre-eclampsia. Even if her BP has been textbook throughout, the combination of late-pregnancy cardiovascular load + a max attempt is a risk profile no responsible programme accepts.

**3. Connective tissue laxity is at its peak.**
Relaxin and other hormones have made ligaments and joint capsules more lax than at any other time in her life. The injury risk profile of a true 1RM in this state is meaningfully elevated, and pregnancy is the worst possible time to take that risk — recovery from any significant injury becomes vastly more complicated.

**4. Coning under maximal load is nearly guaranteed.**
Even with perfect bracing, a true 1RM at 32 weeks will almost certainly cone. Every coning event under max load contributes to DR severity and lengthens postpartum recovery.

**5. It violates her OB clearance.**
This one matters most. If anything went wrong — even something unrelated — you'd be in an indefensible position professionally. The clearance is the clearance.

**6. The stimulus isn't actually what she wants.**
Here's the deeper issue: a 1RM expression at 32 weeks wouldn't be a representation of her actual strength. It would be a representation of her strength as expressed through a compressed diaphragm, a stretched midline, a shifted centre of mass, and a different bracing system. Whatever number she hit, it wouldn't be *her* number. It would be a pregnancy-modified number. That's not satisfying to test, and it's not informative for programming.

## What She Actually Wants From a Peak Week

Let's get at the real need. An advanced lifter at the end of a 12-week block wants:

- To feel like the work added up to something
- A measurable expression of progress
- A satisfying, demanding session that closes the block
- Something to remember and reference going forward

**All of that is available without a 1RM.** Here's how.

## Peak Week — Week 12 (Gestation 31–32)

The original Phase 3 design has her at 3 strength days at RPE 6 — appropriately tapered. For peak week, we don't push intensity higher than the phase allows, but we **make the session feel like an event.** Three tools do the heavy lifting:

### Tool 1: Top Set at the Phase Ceiling

Not a 1RM — a **single working set at the top of her RPE 6 range**, taken with full focus, full setup, full intent. For an advanced lifter, an honest RPE 6 single or triple at 32 weeks is a real expression of strength. It's the heaviest thing she's done in weeks. It will feel like training.

### Tool 2: Rep PR at a Submaximal Load

This is where you actually get a "PR" feeling without violating any rules. Pick a load she's been working with throughout Phase 3 and have her do **an RPE 7 set for reps** (still 2+ RIR, no failure). Document the number. This becomes a benchmark she can chase postpartum.

### Tool 3: A Hard, Memorable Finisher

Carries. Density work. Something that absolutely smokes her without requiring high load or breath holding. This is what she'll actually remember from the session.

## Peak Week Sessions

### Monday — Pressing Peak
- **Low-incline DB press (45°):** work up to a top set of 5 @ RPE 6 — heaviest she's pressed in 4 weeks
- **Low-incline DB press (45°):** 3×8 @ ~80% of that top set, controlled
- **Chest-supported row:** 3×10
- **Standing landmine press:** 3×8/side
- **Finisher:** mechanical drop set — DB fly into press, 3 rounds, no rest between
- **Cable triceps pushdown:** 3×15
- **Pallof press iso hold:** 3×15 sec/side

### Wednesday — Lower Peak
- **Trap bar deadlift:** work up to a top triple @ RPE 6 — heaviest pull in 4 weeks
- **Trap bar deadlift:** 3×5 @ ~80% of that top set
- **Goblet box squat:** 3×6, paused on box
- **B-stance hip thrust:** 3×8/side
- **Finisher: heavy farmer's carry medley** — 4 × 40 sec, push the load. **This is where she gets to feel like a beast.**
- **45° back extension:** 3×10

### Friday — Full Body Peak + Test Day
- **Front-rack goblet squat:** top set of 5 @ RPE 6
- **Low-incline DB press (45°):** rep test — pick a weight she handled at RPE 6 in Week 8, do **one set for reps to RPE 7** (still 2 RIR). Record it.
- **Single-arm DB row:** rep test — same protocol, RPE 7 for reps. Record it.
- **Heavy suitcase carry:** 4 × 30 sec/side, push the load
- **Deep squat hold with breathing:** 3 × 45 sec — labour prep, fitting send-off

The Friday rep tests become her **two benchmark numbers** going into postpartum. When she's cleared to lift again, those become the targets she rebuilds toward. That's a far more useful data point than a pregnancy 1RM would be.

## What "Peaking" Means in This Context

In a normal training block, peaking means tapering volume, holding intensity, and arriving fresh for a max expression. In pregnancy, **peaking means the same taper, but the expression is "an honest hard session at the phase ceiling," not a max.** Same structural logic, different terminal output.

The taper still works:
- Lower volume that week (one fewer set on accessories)
- Full intent on the top sets
- Adequate sleep and food going in
- Same warm-up ritual she'd use for a meet

She'll walk out of Friday's session feeling like she trained. That's the goal.

## The Conversation to Have With Her

Be direct. Something like:

> "I know you want to test a max at the end of this block — I get it, that's how we close a training cycle. Here's where I've landed: a real 1RM at 32 weeks isn't safe and it's not what your OB cleared. But more importantly, whatever number you hit wouldn't actually be *your* number — it would be a pregnancy-compressed expression of your strength, and it wouldn't tell us anything useful.
>
> What I want to do instead: peak week has you working up to top sets at the ceiling we've been building toward, then doing rep tests on bench and row. Those rep numbers become your benchmarks. When you're cleared postpartum, those are the targets we rebuild to, and then we go after real maxes again. That's the test that actually matters."

Most advanced lifters get this when it's framed as deferred testing rather than no testing. **The maxes come back. The pregnancy doesn't repeat. Protect the pregnancy.**

## When She *Can* Test Again

For planning purposes:

- **Postpartum weeks 0–6:** no testing, no real training. Pelvic floor PT, walking, breath work.
- **Weeks 6–12 postpartum:** clearance check, gradual return to lifting, rebuild patterns. Still no maxes.
- **Months 3–6 postpartum:** progressive overload, rebuild working loads, address any DR/PF residuals.
- **Months 6–9 postpartum:** if everything is structurally sound, gradual reintroduction of heavier work, RPE 8 territory.
- **Around 9–12 months postpartum:** first true max attempts, *if* breathing/bracing/pelvic floor all check out. Many lifters PR within 12–18 months of birth.

# 12-Week Prenatal Programme — Full Summary

**Client:** 30 y/o advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant at programme start, finishing at 32 weeks
**Clearance:** OB-approved moderate strength training
**Contraindications:** No supine after week 16, no max attempts, no contact sports

## Universal Rules (Apply Throughout)

**Lifting**
- No supine work — incline benches at 30°+ default
- No 1RM attempts; RPE ceiling 7 (Phase 1, 3) or 8 (Phase 2)
- No Valsalva — exhale through the sticking point
- Watch midline coning on every set; regress if it appears
- Spotter or safeties on all barbell pressing

**Cardio**
- Talk test governs intensity (HR unreliable in pregnancy)
- 150 min/week moderate activity (ACOG)
- No fall risk (no outdoor cycling, no trail running)
- Core temp ceiling 38.5°C

**Recovery**
- Sleep side-lying (left preferred), 8+ hours
- Daily breath + pelvic floor work (5 min)
- Refer to pelvic floor PT now if not already done

**Red Flags — Stop and Call OB**
Vaginal bleeding, regular contractions, fluid leakage, dyspnoea at rest, dizziness, chest pain, calf swelling, decreased fetal movement, severe headache, persistent shortness of breath at low intensity.

# 12-Week Prenatal Programme — Full Summary

**Client:** 30 y/o advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant at programme start, finishing at 32 weeks
**Clearance:** OB-approved moderate strength training
**Contraindications:** No supine after week 16, no max attempts, no contact sports

---

## Universal Rules (Apply Throughout)

**Lifting**
- No supine work — incline benches at 30°+ default
- No 1RM attempts; RPE ceiling 7 (Phase 1, 3) or 8 (Phase 2)
- No Valsalva — exhale through the sticking point
- Watch midline coning on every set; regress if it appears
- Spotter or safeties on all barbell pressing

**Cardio**
- Talk test governs intensity (HR unreliable in pregnancy)
- 150 min/week moderate activity (ACOG)
- No fall risk (no outdoor cycling, no trail running)
- Core temp ceiling 38.5°C

**Recovery**
- Sleep side-lying (left preferred), 8+ hours
- Daily breath + pelvic floor work (5 min)
- Refer to pelvic floor PT now if not already done

**Red Flags — Stop and Call OB**
Vaginal bleeding, regular contractions, fluid leakage, dyspnoea at rest, dizziness, chest pain, calf swelling, decreased fetal movement, severe headache, persistent shortness of breath at low intensity.

---

## Phase 1 — Strength Maintenance (Weeks 1–4 / Gestation 20–23)

**Theme:** Establish template, dial in RPE, baseline carries and rep numbers.

**Split:** 4 strength + 3 cardio

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Upper Push (Heavy Press Day) |
| Tue | Cardio: Zone 2, 35 min |
| Wed | Lower Squat |
| Thu | Cardio: Bike intervals, 30 min (8×60s on / 90s off) |
| Fri | Upper Pull |
| Sat | Lower Hinge |
| Sun | Cardio: Long easy, 45 min |

**Main lifts (RPE 6–7):**
- Low-incline barbell bench (15–30°): 5×5
- Front-rack goblet / front squat or SSB squat: 4×6–8
- Lat pulldown / chest-supported row: 4×8
- Trap bar deadlift: 4×5

**Core focus:** Build the deep stabiliser system. Dead bug, bird dog, Pallof, suitcase carry. ~9–12 sets/week.

**Cardio totals:** ~140–160 min/week

---

## Phase 2 — Higher Intensity Block (Weeks 5–8 / Gestation 24–27)

**Theme:** Push intensity through tempo, clusters, density, and intensity techniques. Same volume, harder work.

**Split:** 4 strength + 3 cardio

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Upper Push (Heavy Press, intensity techniques) |
| Tue | Cardio: Bike intervals, 30 min (8×45s @ RPE 7 / 75s easy) |
| Wed | Lower Squat |
| Thu | Cardio: Hill walking tempo, 35 min (3×7 min @ 8–12% incline) |
| Fri | Upper Pull + secondary press |
| Sat | Lower Hinge |
| Sun | Cardio: Long easy, 45 min |

**Main lifts (RPE 7–8 ceiling):**
- Low-incline barbell bench: 5×4 with 3-sec eccentric, 1-sec pause
- Cluster work added: 2 clusters of (3 reps, 20 sec rest, 3 reps)
- Front squat / front-rack goblet: 5×4 with 3-sec descent
- Trap bar deadlift: 5×4 with 2-sec pause off floor

**Intensity techniques:** 3-sec eccentrics, paused work, 1.5 reps, cluster sets, mechanical drop sets on accessories, tight rest periods for density.

**Core focus:** Heavier carries, anti-rotation under load, isometric holds. Watch for first signs of coning around week 26–27 and regress as needed.

**Auto-regulation:** Morning resting HR >10 bpm above baseline → drop to RPE 6 across the day. Coning, leaking, or Braxton-Hicks during sets → end the session.

**Cardio totals:** ~150–180 min/week

---

## Phase 3 — Stability & Labour Prep (Weeks 9–12 / Gestation 28–31)

**Theme:** Volume down, frequency redistributed, focus shifts to mobility, posterior chain, carries, and breath. Pressing identity preserved through DBs and machines.

**Split:** 3 strength + 4 cardio

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Full Body (Press Emphasis) |
| Tue | Cardio: Easy walk or swim, 30 min |
| Wed | Full Body (Hinge Emphasis) |
| Thu | Cardio: Bike or elliptical, 30 min |
| Fri | Full Body (Accessory + Peak Week sessions) |
| Sat | Cardio: Long easy, 40–50 min |
| Sun | Active recovery: 20–30 min walk + mobility |

**Main lifts (RPE 6 ceiling):**
- Low-incline DB press (45°): 4×8
- Goblet box squat: 3×6
- Trap bar deadlift or KB deadlift: 3×5
- Chest-supported plate-loaded press: 3×10

**Pressing shift:** Barbell pressing becomes awkward around week 28–30. Default to DBs, Smith, plate-loaded machines, landmine. Same pattern, different implement.

**Core focus:** Mostly standing — carries, half-kneeling chops, breath work, deep squat holds. Drop anything that produces coning. Daily post-meal walks (3×10 min) for glucose management.

**Cardio totals:** ~150–170 min/week

---

## Peak Week (Week 12 / Gestation 31–32)

**No 1RM attempts** — outside OB clearance and contraindicated at this stage.

**What replaces it:**
- **Mon:** Top set of 5 on low-incline DB press at RPE 6 (heaviest press in 4 weeks), drop sets, mechanical finisher
- **Wed:** Top triple on trap bar deadlift at RPE 6, heavy farmer's carry medley as the satisfying finisher
- **Fri:** Top set on front-rack goblet squat, then **rep tests at RPE 7** on low-incline DB press and single-arm DB row. These become benchmarks for postpartum return.
- Closes with deep squat holds — direct labour prep.

True maxes return around 9–12 months postpartum once breath, brace, and pelvic floor function are restored.

---

## Pressing Programme (Across All Phases)

- **Phase 1–2:** Low-incline barbell bench (15–30°) as primary; DBs, Swiss bar, landmine as accessories
- **Phase 3:** Low-incline DB press, plate-loaded machine, landmine — same pattern, no barbell
- Heavy pressing 1×/week, secondary press exposure 1×/week
- **Cues:** 30°+ incline, exhale through press, ribs down, no arch, watch midline, spotter or safeties always

---

## Core Programme (Across All Phases)

**Four categories trained weekly:**
1. **Breath & pressure management** — daily 5 min
2. **Anti-extension** — dead bug, bird dog, Pallof (Mon)
3. **Anti-rotation** — chops, half-kneeling press, single-arm carries (Wed)
4. **Anti-lateral flexion** — side plank, suitcase carry (Fri)

**Avoided throughout:** crunches, sit-ups, V-ups, leg raises, ab wheel, Russian twists, GHD work, anything supine after week 16

**Coning is the governor.** If it appears on any movement (core or compound), that movement gets regressed immediately.

---

## Nutrition Plan

**Caloric targets:**
- Phase 1: maintenance + 350 kcal
- Phase 2: maintenance + 400 kcal
- Phase 3: maintenance + 450 kcal

**Macros (for ~65 kg client, scale to her bodyweight):**
- **Protein:** 1.6–1.8 g/kg pre-pregnancy weight (~125–140 g), spread 30–40 g across 4 meals
- **Carbs:** 4–5 g/kg (~260–325 g), loaded around training
- **Fat:** 0.8–1.0 g/kg (~55–65 g), emphasising omega-3 / DHA
- **Fibre:** 28–30 g
- **Fluids:** 3–3.5 L/day + electrolytes around training

**Weight gain target:** 0.75–1 lb/week through T2 and T3 (~25–35 lb total).

**Avoid:** alcohol, raw/undercooked animal products, unpasteurised dairy, high-mercury fish, deli meats unheated, excess caffeine (>200 mg/day), liver in large amounts.

**Key micronutrients to verify:** folate, iron, calcium, vitamin D, **choline** (often missed in prenatals), **DHA** (often under-dosed), iodine.

**Phase 3 nutrition adjustment:** smaller, more frequent meals as stomach capacity drops. Liquid calories (smoothies, milk) become useful. Daily post-meal walks for glucose management.

---

## Cardio Summary

**Throughout:** ~150 min/week moderate activity via Z2 walks, bike, elliptical, swimming.

**Phase 1:** True intervals available (8×60s on bike).
**Phase 2:** Intervals continue, hill tempo added (treadmill 8–12% incline).
**Phase 3:** Drop intervals; shift to swimming, recumbent bike, walking. Daily post-meal walks.

**Always:** talk test governs, electrolytes during sessions ≥30 min, cool environment, immediate stop on red flags.

---

## Weekly Volume At-a-Glance

| Phase | Strength days | Cardio days | Main lift RPE | Core sets/wk | Cardio min/wk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | 4 | 3 | 6–7 | 9–12 | 140–160 |
| Phase 2 | 4 | 3 | 7–8 | 12–15 | 150–180 |
| Phase 3 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 9–12 | 150–170 |

---

## Programme Trajectory

**She arrives:** Advanced lifter, 20 weeks pregnant, used to training hard, wanting to stay strong.

**She leaves (week 32):** Cardiovascularly conditioned, structurally sound, midline managed, pelvic floor coordinated, pressing pattern preserved through DB/machine work, benchmark rep numbers on file for postpartum return, labour-prepared through deep squat work and breath training, and *still feeling like an athlete* — which is the variable that determines whether she comes back to lifting at all postpartum.

**Then:** Birth, ~6–8 week clearance check, pelvic floor PT, progressive return to lifting, rebuilt working loads by month 3–6, RPE 8 work by month 6–9, true maxes back on the table around 9–12 months postpartum.

That's the full arc. Send me her starting numbers on low-incline bench, front squat, and trap bar deadlift and I'll plug in specific Week 1 loads to kick the programme off.
